claims.statement: FPT/GHEC/GHES metadata scopes the runner-risk concept; conditional body sections still govern availability.
The threat analysis assumes an attacker can run malicious commands on a runner; it is not a finding that the owned estate is compromised.
For FPT/GHEC, hosted runners do not scan user-downloaded job code such as a compromised dependency. Hosted isolation is not a promise of malware scanning.

The article distinguishes fork pull_request jobs with read-only permissions/no secrets from other events or same-repository PRs that may expose credentials or write authority. Preserve event and trust-boundary differences.
A malicious runner command can read a secret that has been supplied through its environment. Environment-variable transport is not isolation from untrusted job code.
A secret interpolated directly into an expression can appear in the generated on-disk shell script. Expression placement changes exposure.

A custom action can expose supplied secrets through its argument handling. Referenced secrets and the built-in token can be harvested despite scrubbing unused secrets; library behavior requires review.

Automatic log masking is not a security boundary against deliberate exfiltration: transformed values and outbound network requests can leak runner data. Do not certify confidentiality from clean-looking logs.
An attacker may steal the repository-scoped job token before expiration and use it immediately. Expiry bounds exposure but is not prevention; this does not describe temporary clone-token lifetimes.
A stolen job token may modify repository content or releases if its assigned permissions permit it. Effective permission restriction matters, not merely token type.

The cross-repository paragraph discusses a write-access user able to create or modify workflows and elevate workflow-token permissions. Its broad token-access comparison is qualified by that actor and configuration authority; it does not grant a read-only fork job write access or contradict the earlier fork case.
Enterprise-owned organizations can share Actions through internal repositories; this does not establish private personal-account support or authorize cross-repository data access.
Other tokens or SSH keys can enable privileged cross-repository interactions but may give collaborators unexpectedly broad access; review exact resources and token type.
The source ranks the per-job single-repository GITHUB_TOKEN first and recommends it when possible; that preference does not promise write privileges for every event.
A repository deploy key can provide single-repository Git clone/push access but cannot call REST or GraphQL. Its suitability depends on the required interface.
An App installation can select repositories and fine-grained resource permissions for workflow access. Selection and installation must be reviewed; no live app adoption is inferred.

The source rejects classic PATs in workflows because their broad account/organization reach can indirectly expose access to repository writers. This is source security guidance, not retroactive revocation authority.

If a PAT is needed, the source rejects a personal-account dependency and proposes a dedicated, narrowly granted fine-grained account token; it calls that approach unscalable and prefers alternatives. No new account is authorized here.
The source rejects personal SSH keys in workflows because of broad repository reach, recommending individual deploy keys for Git-only use instead. API access needs a different reviewed credential.
The security-best-practices link is a follow-up reference, not additional review or estate assurance.

scope: Pinned full-article reading with literal includes, selected variables and visual dependencies; source claims only, no adoption or live behavior assertion.
